title: Volunteering at Greenway Nature Reserve
speaker: Guide
text: Good morning, everyone, and thank you for volunteering at Greenway Nature Reserve. I'm Helen, the volunteer coordinator, and I'll explain how things work before you start. The reserve covers about forty hectares, and most of it is wetland, so please keep to the paths. Volunteers usually work in the mornings, from nine until half past twelve, because the birds are more active in the afternoon and we try not to disturb them. You don't need to bring any tools; we provide everything. What you do need are waterproof boots, because even in summer the ground is wet. Some people ask about gloves. We used to ask volunteers to bring their own, but now we supply them, as many people forgot. Lunch isn't provided, but there's a small kitchen in the visitor centre where you can make tea and coffee. Now, the tasks. On Mondays and Tuesdays the main job is clearing paths, which means cutting back plants and repairing the wooden walkways. On Wednesdays we do the bird count. Don't worry if you can't tell one duck from another; you'll be paired with an experienced counter. Thursday is set aside for building nest boxes in the workshop, and on Fridays we run activities for local school groups, so if you enjoy working with children, Friday is the day for you. A few safety points. If you see a fire, don't try to put it out yourself; call the main office straight away. The number is on the back of your badge. And if you're working near the lake, always work with a partner. Finally, the volunteer of the month. Each month we choose one volunteer who has made a special contribution, and they receive a free annual pass to the reserve's café. Last month it went to Peter, who rebuilt the old bridge almost single-handedly.

title: Changes at Millbrook Public Library
speaker: Librarian
text: Hello, and welcome to this short talk about the changes at Millbrook Public Library, which reopens next month after the building work. The biggest change is the opening hours. We used to close at six every evening, but from now on we'll stay open until eight on weekdays, as many of you told us you couldn't get here after work. On Saturdays we'll still close at five, and we remain closed on Sundays, at least for now. Inside, the layout is quite different. When you come in, the information desk is no longer straight ahead. It's now on your left, next to the new self-service machines, where you can borrow and return books yourself. The children's section has moved upstairs to the first floor, which is much quieter for everyone, and there's a lift as well as the stairs. Where the children's books used to be, on the ground floor, there's now a café run by a local charity. We've also created four study rooms. These can be booked online for up to two hours at a time, and they're free for members. Several of you have asked about the computers. We now have thirty, which is double the number we had before, and printing costs ten pence a page in black and white. Colour printing is fifty pence a page. Membership is still free for everyone who lives in the area, but you'll need to bring proof of your address, such as a recent bill, as well as some photo identification. Finally, our events. The reading group meets on the first Tuesday of every month, and the next talk in our local history series will be about the old railway that once ran through the town.

title: Riverside Food Festival
speaker: Presenter
text: And now for some news about this year's Riverside Food Festival, which takes place on the weekend of the fourteenth and fifteenth of June. The festival is moving this year. For the last ten years it was held in the town square, but it has grown so much that it's now going to be in Victoria Park, by the river, where there's room for over a hundred stalls. Entry is free for children under twelve, and adults pay four pounds, which is a pound more than last year. The organisers say the extra money will pay for more seating areas and better toilets, which were the two main complaints last year. Parking near the park is very limited, so visitors are asked to use the park-and-ride service from the football stadium. Buses leave every fifteen minutes and the ticket includes the return journey. As always, there'll be plenty to eat. This year's theme is food from coastal regions, so expect a lot of seafood, but there will also be a large area for vegetarian and vegan food, which proved so popular last year that some stalls ran out by lunchtime. There's also something new: a cookery school tent, where well-known local chefs will give free lessons every hour. Places are limited to twenty people per lesson, and you can't book in advance, so get there early. For children, there's a baking competition on the Sunday morning. Entries must be brought to the main tent by ten o'clock, and the prize is a family meal at one of the festival's sponsor restaurants. And if you'd like to help, the organisers still need volunteers for the Saturday, especially people to collect rubbish and recycling around the site.

title: A tour of Harlow Castle
speaker: Guide
text: Welcome to Harlow Castle. Before we begin the tour, let me give you a little background. The castle was built in the twelfth century, but very little of the original building remains. What you see today mostly dates from the fifteenth century, when the castle was rebuilt after a fire. We're standing in the outer courtyard. The building on your right is the old kitchen, which is now our gift shop. Directly opposite us is the Great Hall, where the family who owned the castle used to hold banquets. It's the largest room in the castle, and it's where you'll find our famous collection of tapestries. Please don't use flash photography in there, as strong light damages the colours. To the left of the Great Hall is the chapel, which is still used for weddings, so it may be closed on some Saturdays. Behind the chapel there's a narrow staircase leading up to the tower. The views from the top are wonderful, but there are a hundred and twelve steps, and the staircase isn't suitable for young children or anyone who finds climbing difficult. If you'd rather not climb, there's a short film about the castle's history in the room at the bottom of the tower, which shows every half hour. Now, the gardens. The gardens were redesigned two years ago, using old drawings to recreate how they looked in the sixteenth century. The herb garden is particularly popular. In the summer months, our gardeners give free talks there at two o'clock every afternoon. One last thing: the castle closes at five, but the last entry to the tower is at four, so if you want to climb it, don't leave it too late.

title: Orientation for new hospital staff
speaker: Manager
text: Good morning, and welcome to your first day at Westfield General Hospital. My name's David Okoro and I manage the staff support team. I'll go through a few practical things now, and you'll have more detailed training in your own departments this afternoon. First, your identity cards. These need to be worn at all times, and they also open the staff doors, so please don't lend yours to anyone. If you lose it, report it to security immediately; a replacement costs fifteen pounds. Next, parking. The staff car park is behind the main building, but it fills up very early, usually by seven thirty. Permits cost twenty pounds a month, and we strongly encourage you to cycle or take the bus if you can. There's secure bicycle storage next to the staff entrance, and showers in the basement. Now, food. The staff restaurant is on the ground floor and it's open twenty-four hours a day, which is unusual, but it means night staff can get a hot meal. Staff get a twenty per cent discount if they show their card. Something many new staff don't know about is our wellbeing service. We offer free, confidential counselling, and also free exercise classes in the evenings. These are very popular, so you'll need to sign up on the staff website. Finally, uniforms. You'll collect your uniform from the laundry department in the basement. You'll be given three sets, and dirty uniforms should be left in the blue bags, not taken home to wash, as this is important for infection control. Right, does anyone have any questions before we take a short break?

title: Ashton Running Club
speaker: Club secretary
text: Hi everyone, thanks for coming along to the open evening for Ashton Running Club. I'm Sue, the club secretary. We've got about two hundred members, and they range from complete beginners to people who run marathons. So, how does the club work? We meet three times a week. On Tuesday evenings we do speed training on the athletics track at the sports centre. Thursday is our social run, which is about eight kilometres at an easy pace, and it always finishes at the café on Bridge Street. Then on Sunday mornings there's a longer run, usually along the canal, and the distance varies depending on what people are training for. If you're new to running, I'd recommend our beginners' course, which starts on the third of September. It lasts ten weeks, and by the end most people can run five kilometres without stopping. The course is led by Mark, who's a qualified coach. Membership costs thirty-five pounds a year, and that includes your entry to the club championship and a club running shirt. If you join before the end of this month, you'll get a ten-pound discount. Many members also enter the races organised by other clubs in the area, and we share transport to those. One thing we're very proud of is that every year the club raises money for a local charity. This year it's the children's hospice, and our target is five thousand pounds. We're doing that mainly through a sponsored relay in October. Safety is important too. In the winter, when it gets dark early, everyone must wear something reflective, and we never let anyone run alone on club runs. Right, if you'd like to sign up, there are forms on the table at the back.

title: The new city cycle hire scheme
speaker: Council officer
text: Good evening. I'm here from the city council to tell you about the new cycle hire scheme, which starts on the first of April. There will be forty docking stations across the city centre, each with between ten and twenty bikes. You'll find stations at the railway station, the university, the hospital and all the main shopping streets. To use the scheme, you first need to register, either through the app or at one of the machines at the docking stations. Registration is free, but you'll need a bank card. After that, the first thirty minutes of every journey are free, and after that it costs one pound for each extra half hour. So for most short trips across the centre, you won't pay anything at all. There are also electric bikes at some stations, which are useful for the hills in the north of the city. These cost a little more: fifty pence to unlock and then the same hourly charges. Some people have asked about helmets. We don't provide them, for hygiene reasons, but we strongly recommend that you wear one. If a bike is damaged, please report it in the app by scanning the code on the handlebars, and don't take it out. When you return a bike, make sure it's pushed firmly into the dock until the light turns green. If it isn't locked properly, the system thinks you still have the bike, and you'll keep paying. The scheme is being paid for partly by sponsorship from a local bank, and partly by the council. If it's successful, a second phase next year will extend it to the suburbs.

title: Holiday activities at Fairfield Community Centre
speaker: Organiser
text: Hello, and thanks for listening to our update on the summer holiday activities at Fairfield Community Centre. This year we're running a five-week programme for children aged six to fourteen, from the twenty-second of July. Each week has a different theme. The first week is all about science, with experiments in our new laboratory room. In week two the theme is art, and the children will be painting a mural on the wall of the car park, which the council has kindly allowed. Week three is sport, which will mostly take place outdoors on the playing field, so please send your children with sun cream and a hat. Week four is drama, and it ends with a performance for parents on the Friday afternoon. The final week is cookery, and the children will learn to make simple, healthy meals. Sessions run from nine in the morning until three in the afternoon. We can also offer early drop-off from eight o'clock, for an extra two pounds a day, for parents who work. The cost is twelve pounds a day, or fifty pounds for a full week, and there's a reduction for families with more than one child. Children should bring a packed lunch, but we provide fruit and water throughout the day. Please don't send any food containing nuts, as several children have allergies. Places are booked on a first-come, first-served basis, and the art and drama weeks are always the first to fill up. You can book online or at reception, and we'll need a contact number and details of any medical conditions when you book.
